transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Chronic Kidney Disease, for Saturday, November 28.
Let's turn to Chronic Kidney Disease, with one preprint today on metabolic memory in diabetic kidney disease.

This comes from the Sandholm lab, posted on medRxiv. The question is whether years of high blood glucose leave a lasting mark on DNA methylation, and whether that mark helps explain why some people with type 1 diabetes go on to develop kidney disease.
They studied 1,245 people with type 1 diabetes from Finland and from the UK and Ireland. They found 17 CpG sites linked to long-term cumulative hyperglycaemia, and the strongest was at TXNIP.

What's interesting is that these methylation signals stayed stable even when short-term glucose changed. That's what you would expect from a molecular record of past exposure, not just a snapshot of current control.

Then they used Mendelian randomization, which suggested that methylation at a CpG in KLF11 has a causal effect on diabetic kidney disease. Kidney chromatin accessibility data and KLF11 expression back that up.

A few cautions. It's a preprint, the cohorts are of European ancestry, and with Mendelian randomization on methylation, instrument strength and pleiotropy are worth checking. The summary also doesn't say whether the findings replicated independently.
Still, tying a methylation mark to kidney regulatory data is a good way to move from association toward mechanism.
The takeaway: cumulative hyperglycaemia seems to leave stable methylation marks, and the one at KLF11 may be a causal epigenetic link between past glucose exposure and diabetic kidney disease.

papers.title: Long-Term Impact of Cumulative Hyperglycaemia on DNA Methylation and its Role in Diabetic Kidney Disease
